doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Facebook live concerts and the physical demands of playing
summary: Juber describes his live-streamed concerts, the audience sizes, that they are not monetizable, and how age, arthritis and a bad back shape how he plays; not travelling and playing electric helps.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah. Technology, yeah. I mean you know especially, I mean I appreciate the fact that we can do this and I can do regular Facebook live concerts by virtue of the technology. I mean you go back fifteen, twenty years, it would not have been the same thing. And being able to play for a, quite a substantial audience. I mean I’ve had anywhere up to seven, eight thousand people on a — especially anything that’s Beatle related tends to draw a much bigger crowd. But regularly — I think yesterday for my Monday session I had I think live was probably about six or seven hundred, and last time I looked it was over two thousand. So, because you’ve got the live audience but then as time shifted too, because it just gets instantly archived, so it’s a way of keeping myself in shape, and also you know maintaining a relationship with an audience but it’s not monetizable, at least not easily monetizable. And it’s not really a piece of business as much as it’s just an artistic exercise.
Okay. Well that’s a good way to put it. One thing I love about your show is what I’m going to call the face chords. Do you know what I’m talking about?

You mean in terms of whatever facial expressions go along with stretches, or, well you know playing guitar is a very physical thing. And you know for me it’s, at my age now, I mean I’m, what am I 67? Yeah 67. The decisions — I have to make certain decisions about like how am I going to sit or stand, and how high is my strap going to be because there’s a certain height where it stresses my left elbow, and if I’m sitting I have to make sure that I don’t — you know it’s either one side or the other is going to get — the arthritis on one side or the spinal, the L4-L5 on the other side. There’s always some kind

of physical thing. But you know to counterbalance that, I’m not having to travel. So it’s not getting on planes. And then more recently I’ve also been playing a lot of electric guitar gigs around L.A. which means I don’t have to schlep a Fender Pro Reverb to the gig, which is, whatever it is, 50, 60 pounds worth of tubes and transformers and speakers and stuff.
